lessons.title: Steam and compressed air
lessons.html:
Steam and compressed air

Utilities are the services that keep the mill running: steam, compressed air, electricity, water and dust extraction. When a utility fails, production stops or quality suffers, so operators must understand and monitor them.

Steam

Steam is used mainly in pellet conditioners, expanders and extruders. It is produced in a boiler fired by coal, gas, diesel or biomass.

  • Quality: conditioners need dry, saturated steam. Wet steam (with water droplets) causes uneven conditioning and die chokes. Steam traps and separators remove condensate.
  • Pressure: boilers produce high-pressure steam that is reduced through a pressure-reducing valve before the conditioner, as the process specifies.
  • Condensate return: returning hot condensate to the boiler saves water, fuel and treatment chemicals.
  • Water treatment: boiler feed water is treated to prevent scale and corrosion; blowdown removes concentrated solids.

Boiler safety

Boilers are pressure equipment regulated under the OHS Act 85 of 1993. They must be inspected and operated by competent, authorised persons. Safety valves, low-water cut-outs and pressure gauges must work and must never be tampered with. Report leaks, unusual noises or alarms immediately. Steam burns are severe; keep lagging (insulation) on pipes and never open steam lines without isolation and depressurising.

Compressed air

Compressed air drives slide gates, diverter valves, filter pulse-cleaning in dust collectors and some packing machines.

  • Air must be dry and clean. Water in air lines causes sticking valves and corrosion; dryers and drain traps remove it.
  • Leaks waste a lot of electricity. Listen for hissing and report leaks.
  • Never point compressed air at a person or use it to clean clothing or skin; it can force air or particles into the body.

lessons.title: Electricity, water and dust extraction
lessons.html:
Electricity, water and dust extraction

Electricity

  • Mills use large motors on hammer mills, pellet mills and fans. Start-up of large motors uses soft starters or variable speed drives to limit current peaks.
  • Power factor correction and efficient motors reduce electricity costs.
  • Load-shedding and outages require planned safe shutdowns. On restart, check for chokes in elevators and conveyors, and start routes in the correct order.
  • Standby generators must be tested regularly and fuel kept in stock.
  • Only qualified electricians work on electrical installations. Operators isolate and lock out at the correct point before mechanical work.

Water

  • Water is used for boilers, liquid additions, cleaning and staff facilities.
  • Process water must be of suitable quality; test as the quality plan requires.
  • South Africa is water-scarce; repair leaks and reuse condensate. Water use is regulated under the National Water Act 36 of 1998.

Dust extraction (aspiration)

Aspiration systems pull dusty air from intake pits, elevators, mills, mixers and coolers through ducting to bag filters or cyclones. They:

  • reduce dust explosion risk;
  • protect worker health and housekeeping;
  • recover product, which is returned to the process.

Monitor filter differential pressure: high pressure means blinded bags; very low may mean torn bags. Check rotary valves and screw conveyors under filters so collected dust is removed. Explosion vents and suppression systems on filters and elevators must be kept clear and maintained.

Other utilities

  • Liquid systems: heated fat and molasses tanks, pumps and meters.
  • Fire protection: hydrants, hose reels and extinguishers inspected regularly.
  • Weighbridge and lighting, often counted as site services.

Key points

  • Conditioners need dry, saturated steam; traps remove condensate.
  • Boiler safety devices must never be tampered with.
  • Compressed air must be dry; never point it at people.
  • Plan safe shutdown and restart for power outages.
  • Dust extraction reduces explosion risk; monitor filter pressure.
